title: Sorting at Scale: Visual Guide
outline: Title: Sorting at Scale: Visual Guide

1. From Heap To Disk | a dataset slider against a fixed 8 GB sort memory, breaking one in-memory sort into ceil(N/M) runs, with four tappable rows mapping earlier topics (memory hierarchy, binary heap, bounded top-k heap, intersecting two sorted lists) onto their job here | external merge sort is those four familiar ideas assembled, and the only new one is that sorted order survives a write

2. Runs And Merge Levels | sliders for run memory M and fan-in F over a 1 TB dataset, plus a replacement-selection toggle, computing runs, merge levels, per-stream buffer size and total I/O | total traffic is 2N(1 + ceil(logF R)), so every merge level costs a full read and a full write, and the largest fan-in is not automatically best because it divides the buffer pool linearly

3. Stepping The Merge | a nine-step walk of the k-way merge over runs A=[2,8,20], B=[1,8,9], C=[3,7,30] showing heads, heap contents and output, plus a K slider comparing K comparisons per record against log2 K | a min-heap turns O(NK) rescanning into O(N log K) with O(K) memory, the invariant is that the global minimum is always a current head, and equal keys need run_id in the comparison to stay deterministic

4. Tuples Become Postings | the same six occurrence tuples from three tiny documents shown in document order, sorted by term only, and sorted by (term, doc_id, position), with the postings and gap encoding each ordering produces | index construction is exactly a sort, and the key must be the full (term, doc_id, position) tuple or postings fragment, gaps go non-positive and duplicates stop being adjacent

5. Sizing A Safe Run | a declared sort budget and an overhead multiplier against an 8 GB worker, showing peak memory, whether the allocation fails mid-sort, and the knock-on run count and merge levels | memory accounting must include pointers, offsets, decoder space and shared headroom, and more smaller valid runs are far cheaper than repeatedly crashing on an oversized one because merge levels grow only logarithmically
